    out=[]
    for i,t in enumerate(tm):
        if t['kind']!='ref': continue
        L=t['tlen']; ids_=[int(x) for x in base['ii'][i,:L]]; p=t['plen']
        pn=set(x.replace(',','').rstrip('.') for x in re.findall(r'\d[\d,]*\.?\d*',byid[t['id']]['problem']))
        prev=set();q=p
        while q<L:
            if ids_[q] in DIG:
                r=q
                while r<L and ids_[r] in DIG: r+=1
                s=''.join(DIG[ids_[x]] for x in range(q,r)); before=Dc(ids_[max(p,q-3):q])
                c='result' if '=' in before[-3:] else ('fromproblem' if s in pn else ('fromearlier' if s in prev else 'othernum'))

For each answer number that exists in its turn's problem, I'll take the query token just before its first digit. Per head, I'll measure attention mass on the exact source digit, on the token before it, on other digits in the same problem, on the rest of the problem, on the answer so far, on earlier turns, and on itself. I'll compare this with ordinary non-number queries as a baseline, and also compute how often the head's largest attention lands exactly on a source token. A head with high source mass and a high hit rate that drops at non-number queries would be a retrieval circuit candidate. If the mass is spread evenly across heads, no single full-layer head holds retrieval.
